title: Pool water clarity and seeing submerged bathers
audience: Pool and spa service workers and operators checking public pools in SA before opening. The figure comes from the South Australian standard; other states have not yet been confirmed, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.
learningOutcomes: Describe the clarity requirement in the South Australian standard, including the test disc and the depth at which it must be visible.
Explain why water clarity is a drowning-prevention control as well as a hygiene control.
Carry out a disc test and decide whether the pool may open.

instruction.heading: What clarity means under the standard
instruction.body: Clarity is how clear or free of cloudiness the water is, and it is judged by how far through the water you can see. The regulations require a 150 mm dark disc, or one that stands out against the floor colour, to be readily seen at the pool's deepest point. Filters strip out suspended and colloidal particles, which is what keeps the water clear. Clarity is a requirement in its own right, not an optional tidy-up step.

instruction.heading: Why clarity is a drowning-prevention control
instruction.body: Clear water lets people estimate depth, see hazards on the floor, and notice someone who has slipped under. The standard also asks for light-reflective internal surfaces, because they help staff notice murky water, sloppy cleaning and swimmers lying under the surface. When the water is cloudy at the deep end, a submerged person can be invisible to lifeguards and fellow bathers. Treat any clarity failure as a safety failure, not only a cosmetic one.

instruction.heading: Doing the disc test
instruction.body: Use a disc that meets the size and colour rule, and lower it to the pool's deepest point. Check that it is clearly visible from the pool edge in the lighting that the public will have. If it cannot be seen, the pool fails the clarity requirement and stays shut to bathers until the water passes. Record the result, the depth tested, the time and the lighting. Then identify the likely cause, such as filter performance, turnover, chemistry, debris or a cleaning gap, and pass it to the operator.

instruction.heading: When clarity fails
instruction.body: A failed disc test is a reason to keep the pool closed, not a reason to test again until it passes by luck. Fix the cause first, which may need a filter check, more circulation, chemistry correction or debris removal. Retest after the fix and before reopening. Do not dilute the test by moving the disc to a shallower spot or by changing its colour.

procedure: Confirm the disc size and colour rule before you start, and check the disc is clean.
Lower the disc to the pool's deepest point and check its visibility from the pool edge.
Record the result, the depth, the time and the lighting conditions.
If the disc is not visible, keep the pool shut to bathers and notify the operator in writing.
After the cause is fixed, retest from the same deepest position before reopening.

workedExamples.situation: An evening check of a 2.5 m deep public pool finds the disc disappears well before the deep end. The pool is due to open for a swim session at 6 am.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the pool open, and what goes in the record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The clarity requirement is not met, and submerged bathers could not be seen. The pool stays closed. Record the failed disc test, the depth reached and the lighting, then tell the operator. Retest after the filtration and circulation have been checked and corrected.

equipmentAndPpe: 150 mm disc, matt black or in a colour that stands out against the pool floor, kept clean
Measuring tape or depth marker for the deepest point
Non-slip footwear and eye protection if chemicals are present at the pool edge

commonErrors.error: Testing from the shallow end and recording a pass.
commonErrors.prevention: The disc must be checked at the pool's deepest point.

commonErrors.error: Using a disc of a different size and calling the result a pass.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the 150 mm disc and the required colour contrast, and note the disc used.

commonErrors.error: Testing under lighting that is brighter than the public will have.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the lighting. If the pool is used at dusk, test at dusk too.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A cloudy pool can hide a submerged bather. Keep the pool closed until the clarity test passes.
Keep the pool edge dry and clear. Wet pool surfaces are slippery.
Figure applies to South Australian public pools under the standard (revised 2013). Confirm the current regulation text.

qualityStandard: The disc test is carried out at the pool's deepest point, with the correct disc.
Any failed result keeps the pool closed until a passing retest is recorded.
Each test record shows the depth, time, lighting and result.
documentationEvidence: Clarity test record with disc used, depth, lighting, time and result
Escalation note and retest record after corrective action
summary: The disc must be readily seen at the pool's deepest point, under the standard's rule.
Clarity protects bathers, because submerged people must be seen.
A failed test keeps the pool closed until a passing retest is recorded.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where must the test disc be checked to meet the clarity requirement?
options: At the midpoint of the longest lane

knowledgeChecks.question: A test disc cannot be read at the pool's deepest point. What is the correct action?
options: Open the pool and monitor the bathers closely and let the bathers continue for now
Move the disc to a shallower spot and retest and then let the bathers back in
Keep the pool shut to bathers, escalate, and retest after the cause is fixed
Record a pass because the water looks blue from the edge and the bathers are happy

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is water clarity treated as a drowning-prevention control, not just a hygiene control?
options: Because clear water reduces the need for lifeguards and it makes the pool look nicer
Because it lets people estimate depth, see hazards and detect submerged users
Because clear water is a sign the heater is set correctly and the pump is working
Because the regulations fix the floor colour and the lights and the signs

sourceReferences: Standard for the Operation of Swimming Pools and Spa Pools in SA (revised 2013), section 4 Water clarity and section 1 Introduction; rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)
